questions.prompt: Find \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) for a gas with \(M=2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\) at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\).
For a Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, order \(v_{\mathrm{mp}}\), \(\bar v\), and \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) from smallest to largest.
questions.answer:
For a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution,
\[
v_{\mathrm{mp}}<\bar v<v_{\mathrm{rms}}
\]

questions.prompt: If a gas temperature is increased from \(300\,\mathrm{K}\) to \(1200\,\mathrm{K}\), by what factor does \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) change?
questions.answer:
\[
v_{\mathrm{rms}}\propto\sqrt{T}
\]
The temperature factor is
\[
\frac{1200}{300}=4
\]
so the speed factor is
\[
\sqrt4=2
\]

questions.prompt: Find the most probable speed of nitrogen at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\), using \(M=2.8\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\).
Find the mean speed of helium at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\), using \(M=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\).
At the same temperature, gas A has molar mass \(M\) and gas B has molar mass \(9M\). Find \(\bar v_A/\bar v_B\).
questions.answer:
Mean speed scales as
\[
\bar v\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}
\]
so
\[
\frac{\bar v_A}{\bar v_B}=\sqrt{\frac{9M}{M}}=3
\]

questions.prompt: A gas has molecular radius \(1.5\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}\) and number density \(2.5\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). Estimate its mean free path using \(\lambda=1/[4\sqrt2\pi r^2(N/V)]\).
A molecule has mean free path \(8.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m}\) and speed \(500\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Estimate its mean free time.
Explain why \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) is more directly connected to average kinetic energy than the mean speed \(\bar v\).
questions.answer:
Translational kinetic energy depends on \(v^2\):
\[
K=\frac12m_0v^2
\]
Therefore the average kinetic energy depends on \(\langle v^2\rangle\), not on \(\langle v\rangle\). The RMS speed is defined by
\[
v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\langle v^2\rangle}
\]
so it connects directly to \(\langle K\rangle=\frac12m_0v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\).

questions.prompt: A gas is compressed isothermally so its number density doubles. In the hard-sphere model, derive how the mean free path and mean free time change, assuming the characteristic molecular speed is unchanged.
questions.answer:
In the hard-sphere model,
\[
\lambda=\frac{1}{4\sqrt2\pi r^2(N/V)}
\]
so \(\lambda\) is inversely proportional to number density. If \(N/V\) doubles,
\[
\lambda_2=\frac{\lambda_1}{2}
\]
For isothermal compression, the speed distribution is unchanged in the ideal-gas model, so a characteristic speed \(v\) is unchanged. Since
\[
t_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac{\lambda}{v}
\]
the mean free time also halves:
\[
t_{\mathrm{mean},2}=\frac{t_{\mathrm{mean},1}}{2}
\]

questions.prompt: At what temperature would helium \((M=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}})\) have the same \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) as nitrogen \((M=2.8\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}})\) at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\)?
For nitrogen at \(300\,\mathrm K\), compare \(v_{\mathrm{mp}}\), \(\bar v\), and \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) using their formula factors.
questions.answer:
For one gas at one temperature,
\[
v_{\mathrm{mp}}=\sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}},\quad \bar v=\sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}},\quad v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}
\]
The numerical factors are \(2\), \(8/\pi=2.55\), and \(3\), so
\[
v_{\mathrm{mp}}<\bar v<v_{\mathrm{rms}}
\]

questions.prompt: A gas has mean free path \(1.2\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm m\) and mean speed \(480\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Estimate the collision frequency.
questions.answer:
Mean free time is
\[
t=\frac{\lambda}{\bar v}
\]
so collision frequency is
\[
f=\frac{1}{t}=\frac{\bar v}{\lambda}
\]
Thus
\[
f=\frac{480}{1.2\times10^{-7}}=4.0\times10^9\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}
\]

questions.prompt: A gas expands isothermally to four times its original volume with the same number of molecules. How do mean free path and mean free time change?
questions.answer:
Number density \(N/V\) falls by a factor of \(4\). Since
\[
\lambda\propto\frac{1}{N/V}
\]
the mean free path increases by a factor of \(4\). At constant temperature, characteristic speed is unchanged, so
\[
t_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac{\lambda}{v}
\]
also increases by a factor of \(4\).

questions.prompt: A gas has molecular radius doubled while number density and temperature stay fixed. In the hard-sphere model, how does mean free path change?
questions.answer:
The hard-sphere estimate is
\[
\lambda=\frac{1}{4\sqrt2\pi r^2(N/V)}
\]
so \(\lambda\propto1/r^2\). Doubling \(r\) increases \(r^2\) by \(4\), so the mean free path becomes one quarter as large.

questions.prompt: Derive \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{3RT/M}\) from \(\langle K_{\mathrm{tr}}\rangle=3k_BT/2\).
questions.answer:
For one molecule,
\[
\langle K_{\mathrm{tr}}\rangle=\frac12m_0v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac32k_BT
\]
Thus
\[
v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac{3k_BT}{m_0}
\]
Using \(m_0=M/N_A\) and \(R=N_Ak_B\),
\[
v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac{3RT}{M}
\]
so
\[
v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}
\]

questions.prompt: Explain why the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution broadens and shifts right as temperature increases.
questions.answer: Increasing temperature raises average translational kinetic energy. Since kinetic energy depends on \(v^2\), more molecules occupy higher speeds. The distribution shifts to larger characteristic speeds and broadens because a wider range of speeds becomes thermally probable.

questions.prompt: A gas mixture contains helium and argon at the same temperature. Explain why their speed distributions are different but their average translational kinetic energies are the same.
questions.answer:
Thermal equilibrium gives each species the same average translational kinetic energy:
\[
\langle K_{\mathrm{tr}}\rangle=\frac32k_BT
\]
Helium has smaller molecular mass, so it must have larger typical speeds to have the same average kinetic energy. Argon is heavier and has a lower speed distribution.

questions.prompt: Derive the dependence of mean free path on pressure for an ideal gas at fixed temperature and molecular radius.
questions.answer:
For hard spheres,
\[
\lambda\propto\frac{1}{N/V}
\]
The molecular ideal-gas equation gives
\[
p=\frac{N}{V}k_BT
\]
At fixed \(T\), \(N/V\propto p\). Therefore
\[
\lambda\propto\frac{1}{p}
\]
Increasing pressure decreases mean free path.

questions.prompt: Why is \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) not the same as the speed of every molecule, and why is that distinction important?
questions.answer: \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) is a statistical average based on \(\langle v^2\rangle\). Individual molecules constantly collide and have a distribution of speeds. The distinction matters because pressure, kinetic energy, collision rates, and escape fractions depend on different averages or on the distribution shape, not on one common speed.
